title: The Sistine ceiling (1508–1512)
hook: Michelangelo paints creation, the hand of God reaching to Adam's

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Renaissance popes, told honestly. Your line was the church has sinned.

High above the floor of a chapel in the Vatican, a man stands on a scaffold with his head bent back and his arm raised, paint dripping onto his face. He thinks of himself as a sculptor. In a comic poem about the job, he complains of his aching neck and his beard pointing up at heaven, and insists he's no painter. The pope who hired him was Julius the Second, yesterday's pope in armor. The painter was Michelangelo.
screen: `A MAN ON A SCAFFOLD, HEAD BENT BACK.` → `I AM NO PAINTER.` → `HIRED BY JULIUS THE SECOND.`

segments.voice: Start with the ceiling. Michelangelo filled it with the opening chapters of Genesis: God dividing light from darkness, the sun and moon, Adam, Eve, the fall, Noah. Prophets and sibyls sit around the edges, as if waiting. Next, the famous panel. Genesis says, in the Douay-Rheims, "God created man to his own image." And in its second telling: "the Lord God formed man of the slime of the earth: and breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul." Michelangelo doesn't paint breath. He paints hands. Then, the gap. Adam lies on bare ground, his arm lifted, his hand loose at the wrist. God rushes toward him through the air, arm stretched out, finger extended. And the two fingers don't touch. There's a sliver of empty ceiling between them. Michelangelo never explained it. Some readers see the instant before life passes across. Others notice the contrast: God straining forward, Adam barely lifting a finger. Others see the whole human story in that gap, made for God and not quite reaching. Finally, why it still matters. The Sistine Chapel is still a working chapel, and the cardinals gather under this ceiling to elect a pope. Yesterday's honest list included Julius. Today's includes what he paid for. The Church holds both, and the ceiling holds both hands, almost touching.
screen: `GENESIS ON THE CEILING.` · `FORMED, AND GIVEN THE BREATH OF LIFE.` · `TWO HANDS, AND A GAP.` · `STILL A WORKING CHAPEL.` · then, large: `ALMOST TOUCHING.`

segments.voice: Find the Creation of Adam on a screen or in memory, or hold your own two hands out in front of you, fingertips almost meeting, and look at the gap while your breath slows. Ask which hand is closer to your day: the one reaching hard, or the one barely lifting. If you pray, let the words from Genesis, the breath of life, ride on your breathing; if not, rest in the space between.
Michelangelo. The sculptor-turned-painter who filled the pope's chapel ceiling with Genesis, where God's hand reaches for Adam's and doesn't quite touch. Today's word.
Your line: almost touching. Some gaps are worth looking at for a long time. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The Sistine Chapel is still used for papal liturgies, and the cardinals meet there in conclave to elect a new pope; pilgrims and visitors are asked to keep silence beneath the ceiling.

notes: Confirm Douay-Rheims (Challoner) wording of Genesis 1:27 and 2:7.

Michelangelo's sonnet to Giovanni da Pistoia paraphrased (bent neck, beard toward heaven, paint dripping on his face, 'I am no painter'); the hook's screen head 'I AM NO PAINTER' paraphrases his closing line. Confirm acceptable.
Myth item: the lying-on-his-back image is a later popular idea; the sonnet and its marginal sketch show him working upright with head bent back. Confirm wording.
Facts to confirm: commissioned by Julius II; Genesis scenes, prophets and sibyls; conclaves held in the Sistine Chapel. Index title dates kept; none stated in the voice.
Interpretations of the gap attributed to 'some readers'/'others'; no claim about Michelangelo's intent.
